1:
Keil calls the kid simply a customary present of the time, and Ellicott finds the same gift given by Judah to Tamar, and grudged in the complaint of the elder brother who was never given one. Henry reads it as a token: the value was inconsiderable, but such things were then used when those at variance were brought together again. He thinks it generously done, since Samson was the party offended and the superior relation, so that she was bound to sue for peace — whence, in quarrels between near relations, those are ever the wisest and best who are most forward to forgive and most willing to stoop for peace' sake.

The father's excuse divides them three ways, and the split is not the usual one. Henry allows him nothing: he had a very ill opinion of Samson, measuring a Nazarite by the common temper of the Philistines, and made the worst of jealousies patronize the worst of robberies — it will never bear us out in doing ill to say that we thought others designed ill. Clarke takes the opposite view twice over: Samson had in fact given great cause to be thought hateful, and in offering the younger daughter the father appears to have been perfectly sincere. Ellicott divides the question. The supposition was reasonable, Samson having left his wife in anger straight after the wedding feast; the conduct was not, for an honourable man could have done no less than restore the dowry Manoah had given, the offer of the sister being an attempt to find some equivalent for a dower he had wrongly kept. Gill and Ellicott both linger over the vehemence of the Hebrew, which says saying I said and in hating thou hast hated her — affirmed, in Gill's reading, confidently and constantly. Henry alone explains the refusal of the younger sister as a point of law, Samson knowing better than to take a wife to her sister; and he alone reads the revenge as public, since a man pleading his own cause would have chastised his rival and his father-in-law and no one else, whereas Samson looks on himself as a public person and on the affront as done to the nation.

What Samson caught is the standing crux, and the bench divides evenly. Gill argues for foxes: the country abounded with them, several places took their names from Shual, a traveller reports them swarming in the hedges and ruins, and being pernicious to vines they may be supposed numerous about Timnath. He adds three reliefs: Samson need not have caught them all himself, nor all in one day, and a creature very like a fox went there two hundred in company. Clarke gathers the same defences and adds the argument from spectacle: where such beasts were scarcer, great multitudes have still been shown at once — Sylla exhibiting a hundred lions to the Roman citizens, Pompey nearly six hundred, one emperor a thousand ostriches and a thousand stags at a time. He then reports the objection fairly: the number is improbable and the use of them stranger still, since animals tied tail to tail would pull contrary ways and stand still. Keil and Ellicott answer by changing the animal. The word covers jackals, which resemble foxes and are still classed with them by the common Arabs, are found in quantities at Joppa and Gaza, herd together and may easily be caught; Ellicott hears them howling in herds about those regions at night, and says it would be hard to catch three hundred foxes but not three hundred of these. He also answers the mechanical objection without naming it: the firebrands were resinous wood loosely trailed between the tails, and the object of tying two beasts together was precisely to impede their motion a little, so that they should not dart away so violently as to put the torch out.
5:
Ellicott alone reconstructs the arson as a scene. It was probably done at night, when nobody would be at hand to quench it, and we may imagine him watching the trails of fire from his rocky fastness and exulting as the conflagration reddened the night. To burn an Arab's crops is still the deadliest of injuries, and it was the method Absalom used to force an interview with Joab. He also produces the closest pagan parallel and refuses the use commonly made of it: at the Roman Cerealia torches were yearly tied to foxes let loose in the circus, in memory of a young man at Carseoli whose burning of a marauding fox sent it into the corn to fire the standing crops — but any attempt to connect that custom with Samson's revenge is quite untenable, and it serves only to show the thing possible. Gill supplies the mechanism, that foxes fear fire and would run for the first shelter with it burning at their tails; Keil marks the extent, from the shocks of wheat to the standing grain and the olive gardens.

Why the Philistines then burned the woman and her father splits them evenly. Clarke thinks it was done to appease Samson, whom they saw to have been unjustly treated by both wife and father-in-law, destroying them to make his wrath cease; Gill reads it the same way, that they thought thus to appease a man they feared. Ellicott puts the question directly and answers no. Looking with fury at blackened fields that a few days before were thick with golden corn, it is inconceivable that the Philistines were in a mood to do justice for the sake of the deadly enemy who had done it; their motive is to insult and injure Samson. He rejects a third explanation, that they had in mind burning as the Jewish penalty for adultery, since to burn a man with his house seems to have been the ordinary revenge of those days. Keil takes the same side and adds a verdict none of the others offers: they burned the house down over its occupants, an act of barbarity that fully justified Samson's war.

How Samson smote them is the last thing at issue. Gill offers three constructions — that he struck their hips and thighs with his hands, having no weapon; or kicked them about; or that the phrase is proverbial for laying on at a great rate — and doubts the Targum's horse and foot, there being no sign of a regular army in the field. Clarke prefers the grappling: with no weapon he must close and, after the manner of wrestlers, trip up their feet and bruise them to death. Ellicott dismisses both, denying that it can mean cavalry and infantry or refer to wrestling at all, and canvasses a darker origin: some fierce custom like the Greek one in which the extremities of a corpse were cut off and laid under the armpits. Keil is content that it is proverbial for unsparing slaughter, with a German and an Arabic phrase to match. Ellicott adds the deflation the chapter keeps inviting: it is nowhere implied that Samson was alone in these raids. On the refuge they divide again. Clarke places Etam in Simeon on the borders of Dan and thinks it fortified; Keil looks to the town between Bethlehem and Tekoah that Rehoboam fortified; Ellicott leaves the site uncertain but corrects the description: it should be a ravine or cave of the cliff, not the top of a rock, since men could not go down to a summit, the word is rendered cleft elsewhere, and this makes sense of his going down here and being brought up afterwards. Such cliff-caves, he adds, are the natural refuge of oppressed peoples, are often fed by springs, and can be held by one man against a multitude.
9:
Ellicott alone doubts the etymology the chapter itself supplies. The name Lehi is used here before the incident from which the place is said to have taken it, exactly as Hormah is used before its own naming; and since tooth is elsewhere the name of an isolated sharp rock, jaw would not be an unnatural name for a range of such rocks. So the name may have existed already and the play on words been fitted to the incident afterwards — though he reports honestly that Josephus says the place had no name before. Keil takes the site as untraceable, dismissing the early church tradition about it as utterly worthless, and passes on one modern identification with a fortified hill on the road to Beersheba.

On the betrayal the bench is unanimous in verdict and various in explanation. Henry is fiercest. Of Judah were they? Degenerate branches of that valiant tribe, utterly unworthy to carry in their standard the lion of the tribe of Judah. He offers two motives and prefers the second: perhaps they were disaffected because Samson was not of their tribe, and out of a foolish fondness for their forfeited precedency would rather be oppressed by Philistines than rescued by a Danite — the church's deliverance has often been obstructed by such jealousies — but rather they stood in awe of the Philistines. Had their spirits not been cowed by their sins and troubles they would have taken so fair an opportunity, with such a man to head them, to struggle for liberty; but sin dispirits men, nay, it infatuates them, and hides from their eyes the things that belong to their peace. Ellicott reaches the same figure independently, measuring how far the Lion Tribe had sunk by this reproach against the national hero and still more by the baseness of betraying him: he finds no sympathy, there are no patriots in search of heroes, and what might not these three thousand have achieved had they been like Gideon's three hundred? Samson, he adds, was not of Judah, which seems to have been living in contented servitude. Keil says it as a reproach too: instead of crowding round a deliverer the Lord had raised up, they were so degraded as to cast his rescue at him as a fault. Henry alone lifts the scene off its own ground, seeing in the army sent against one man who was himself an army the band that came to seize a greater deliverer, when a tenth would have served because his hour was come, and ten times as many would have done nothing had he not yielded.

The direction of the journey is disputed again. Gill notes that the text has them going up to the top of the rock while the Greek and Latin versions have them going down into the cave, which one authority takes for a cave dug in the rock; two verses later he registers the tension the other way about. Ellicott simply corrects it to a going down, adding that they would easily gain information about the hiding place. On the numbers they agree: Gill says three thousand was a large party to take one man, the reason being that they knew his strength, and Clarke infers that he was strongly posted and they thought no fewer would reduce him. Clarke also gives the Philistine calculation, that they wished no open rupture with Israel provided the author of their disasters were handed over. On the oath Samson exacts, Ellicott supposes him parleying from some point of vantage he could have held for a time, and Clarke supplies the reason he asked for it: he could not bear the thought of contending with and slaying his own countrymen, there being no doubt he could have freed himself from their hands as easily as from the enemy's.
13:
Two of them reverse here what one of them argued three verses back. Keil takes the naming as proleptic: the place is called Lehi at the start, but first received the name from this deed, when Samson threw the bone away and called the spot the jaw-bone height. Gill says the same in passing, that it was afterwards so called from what happened there, and puts it six miles from Etam. Ellicott had argued the contrary; here he lets it stand and turns to the cave, asking whether it lay down the steep face of a cliff, as such caves do, and citing the brigands' caves that could be attacked neither from below nor above until soldiers were let down in chests.

The loosing of the cords is heard by both the grammarians as verse. Keil says the cords became like threads burnt with fire and the fetters melted from his hands, the description rising into poetical parallelism to depict the triumph. Ellicott presses harder: the shout was a cheer of welcome and not a war cry, the verb an onomatopoeia like our own hurrah, and the bands did not merely loose but melted or flowed off — whence he concludes that the colour and rhythm of the narrative are influenced by some lost poem on Samson's deeds.

What kind of jawbone it was divides them by degrees. Gill takes new to mean lately killed, still moist with the matter of the wound as the physicians use the word, and so tough enough to strike with where an old bone would be brittle — the asses of those countries being perhaps larger than ours. Ellicott says the same more briefly, and alone notices the difficulty it raises, that a Nazarite was forbidden to touch a carcase and Samson must here have felt himself absolved. Clarke goes past both and argues from the economy of the narrative: the word should mean the putrid state of the animal, so that finding a dead ass in putrefaction he could the more easily separate the jaw from its integuments — a circumstance worth recording, where a bone freshly parted from a head would not be. Ellicott also lightens the number, since the verb is smote rather than slew and the expression is general, as when Saul is said to have slain his thousands; and one man daring to rush on them with so wretched a weapon would set them flying the faster.

The song at the end is where they part most sharply. Keil keeps a heap, two heaps and draws from the doubling an inference nobody else makes, that the thousand fell not in one encounter but in several, the Philistines fleeing in awe of a man who had burst his bonds while he smote heap after heap as he overtook them. Clarke rejects the received rendering outright and offers his own, that it should run with the jawbone of this ass, an ass of two asses, and with the jawbone of this ass I have slain a thousand men. Ellicott rejects it too and rebuilds the couplet as a pun, turning on the identity of sound between the words for a heap and for an ass and the play between the words for a thousand and for an ox, which he renders, clumsily by his own admission, as smiting an ox-load of men with the jaw of the ass. He then defends the punning against the charge of levity, since such play often arises out of deep emotion — as when a dying man in the play answers the king who asks whether sick men can play so nicely with their names, that misery makes sport to mock herself — and quotes the judgment that a nation whose sons could still flow out in such vivacity felt itself unsubdued, these casual and teasing humiliations beginning to deliver it.
17:
Whether the thirst was a natural consequence or a rebuke divides them four to one. Clarke calls it the natural consequence of excessive fatigue; Ellicott adds only that it was harvest heat and he had pursued till he was exhausted; Keil the same, the pursuit and the conflict having spent him in hot summer weather. Gill reports the older opinion, that the thirst came as a rebuke for ascribing the victory to his own strength, and rejects it: there seems no foundation for it, thirst being no wonder in a man who had been bound with cords, exerted himself so, killed a thousand with his own hand and then sung a triumph over it. Henry takes the opinion up and makes it his own. God would hereby keep him from being proud of his strength and let him know that he was but a man; the chastisement fell because he had not mentioned God in the memorial of his victory but taken all the praise to himself, so that now, ready to die for thirst, he is under a sensible conviction that his own arm could not have saved him. He adds the line that fixes it: Samson had drunk largely of the blood of the Philistines, but blood will never quench any man's thirst. He also turns the moment back on the men of Judah, who might have met their conqueror with bread and wine as Melchizedek met Abram, and instead left their deliverer ready to perish for a draught of water: thus are the greatest slights often put upon those who do the greatest services. And on the prayer: those who forget to attend God with praises may be compelled to attend him with prayers.

Where the water came from is the last crux, and Ellicott is scathing. The notion that God made a fountain in one of the tooth-sockets of the ass's jawbone is, he says, one of the childish misinterpretations with which the exegesis of Scripture is constantly defaced. Lehi is the name of the place; and if the spring is called a tooth-socket, that is only the play on words which runs through the narrative, since once the cliff had got the name Jawbone the spring would naturally be called a socket. Clarke reaches the same end by a shorter road: the fountain is said to be in Lehi unto this day, and therefore cannot have been in the jawbone of an ass, which is a most unfortunate rendering. Keil places it simply at Lechi, God splitting the hollow so that water came out as at Horeb and Kadesh. Gill hesitates. He gives the socket reading first, a grinder knocked from its place leaving a hollow in the form of a mortar, remarking that from such a place blood would naturally have issued rather than water; then reports the version that has God cleave the rock in the jaw; and ends by supposing that the place on which the bone was cast was a rock, and that God clave a hollow there.

The smaller questions are left open. Ellicott gives three derivations of the place-name and prefers the plainest, the hill of Lehi, over the lifting up and the casting away of the jawbone, the last requiring a different form; and of the twenty years he can say only that they were probably the vague prerogatives of a military hero, and that why the verse stands here and again at the end of the next chapter we cannot say. Clarke reports a variant of forty years and dismisses it, no manuscript or version acknowledging it, and passes on the reckoning that the twenty began in the eighteenth year of the servitude. Gill keeps the qualification that Samson only began to deliver Israel and was no author of a perfect salvation, though a check upon the Philistines and a preservative from idolatry.
